issues.legal_issue: The market value of acquired land may be determined by relying on nearby sale transactions and making a fact-sensitive adjustment for differences between the sale land and the acquired land, without applying a fixed deduction.
material_facts: The appeals challenged compensation determined for two sets of land acquisitions.
The High Court relied on sale transactions involving land within 20 killas or less of the acquired land and on evidence about the acquired land's location and potential.
The acquired land was found to be next to municipal limits and near a golf course, with potential for residential or commercial development.

The High Court applied a 20% deduction and rejected the request for a greater deduction; it disregarded a sale of a constructed house because there was no evidence of the value of the land beneath it.
The Union of India argued that the relied-on sales concerned better-located land and that a greater deduction was warranted. The landowners accepted the compensation fixed by the High Court.
The Supreme Court found no error of principle in the High Court's approach and dismissed the appeals.
issues.conclusion: The compensation determinations were not interfered with because the High Court's reliance on the sale transactions and its assessment of the appropriate deduction were justified on the evidence and circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 4 and 23(1) of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, market value is assessed as of the date of publication of the Section 4 notification. A bona fide sale to a willing buyer can be used when it is sufficiently close in time and situation and the land has comparable advantages; suitable adjustments must be made for relevant differences, but no fixed deduction applies in every case. The court considers the facts as a prudent purchaser would, including the land's location, development potential, size, and development needs. The Court relied on Chimanlal Hargovinddas v. Special Land Acquisition Officer, Poona; Viluben Jhalejar Contractor v. State of Gujarat; Basavva v. Special Land Acquisition Officer; Bhagwathula Samanna; L. Kamalamma; Administrator General of West Bengal v. Collector; K.S. Shivadevamma v. Assistant Commissioner and Land Acquisition Officer; Hasanali Khanbhai & Sons v. State of Gujarat; Land Acquisition Officer v. Nookala Rajamallu; Kasturi v. State of Haryana; Tejumal Bhojwani v. State of U.P.; V. Hanumantha Reddy v. Land Acquisition Officer; H.P. Housing Board v. Bharat S. Negi; Kiran Tandon v. Allahabad Development Authority; and Registrar, University of Agricultural Sciences. It distinguished Basant Kumar v. Union of India, Indumati Chitaley v. Union of India, and Special Land Acquisition Officer v. Karigowda on their facts, while accepting their stated propositions.

rule.if: compensation_appeal and comparable_sale_transactions_used and acquired_land_has_development_potential and acquired_land_is_near_developed_area and adjustment_assessed_on_case_facts

predicates.compensation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging compensation determined for acquired land.
predicates.comparable_sale_transactions_used: The court relied on sale transactions involving land sufficiently close in time and situation to the acquired land.
predicates.acquired_land_has_development_potential: The acquired land was found to have potential for residential or commercial development.
predicates.acquired_land_is_near_developed_area: The acquired land was found to be near a developed area or municipal limits.
predicates.adjustment_assessed_on_case_facts: The court assessed the adjustment by considering the evidence and relevant differences between the sale land and the acquired land.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerning compensation for acquired land involves comparable sales, development potential, proximity to a developed area, and a case-specific assessment of adjustments, the compensation determination is not interfered with.
